title: Episode 12: The Pig War of 1859: The Standoff Over a Rooting Hog
description:
In June 1859, on San Juan Island in the Pacific Northwest borderlands of the Oregon Territory, an American settler shot a British Berkshire pig rooting in his potato patch. The dispute escalated into a military standoff with five British warships, 167 guns, and Captain George Pickett's American troops, nearly sparking war between global superpowers.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In nineteenth-century geopolitics, wars between great empires were fought over gold mines, ocean trade routes, and imperial honor. Yet, in the summer of eighteen fifty-nine, the United States of America and the British Empire came within a hair's breadth of total war in the rugged, foggy waters of the Pacific Northwest—all over an errant, black Berkshire pig that wandered into an American settler's potato patch. It involved future Civil War heroes, Royal Navy battleships bristling with heavy cannon, and a British admiral who refused to blow up the world over bacon. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE AMBIGUOUS TREATY OF 1846
In eighteen forty-six, after decades of fierce diplomatic posturing under the aggressive expansionist slogan 'Fifty-Four Forty or Fight,' the United States and the British Empire signed the historic Oregon Treaty, peacefully partitioning the Pacific Northwest along the forty-ninth parallel from the crest of the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. However, when the diplomats in London and Washington reached the jagged, island-strewn coastline of Puget Sound and the Strait of Georgia, they faced an archipelago of rugged, pine-covered islands that completely defied simple cartography. The treaty vaguely specified that the maritime boundary should follow the forty-ninth parallel to the middle of the channel which separates the continent from Vancouver Island, and thence southerly through the middle of said channel to Fuca's Straits. Unfortunately for international peace, the diplomats had relied upon crude, incomplete eighteenth-century navigational charts prepared by George Vancouver, failing to realize that there was no single channel separating the landmasses. To the west lay Haro Strait, running along the rugged eastern coastline of Vancouver Island; to the east lay Rosario Strait, hugging the rocky mainland coast of Washington Territory. Sitting directly between them, like a disputed emerald in the cold coastal fog, was San Juan Island—a fertile, strategically vital landmass of fifty-five square miles guarding the maritime approaches to the Fraser River. The British Crown asserted that Rosario Strait was the intended boundary, making San Juan Island sovereign British territory under the colonial jurisdiction of British Columbia. The United States insisted with equal fervor on Haro Strait, claiming the island as sovereign American soil within Washington Territory. For thirteen uneasy years, both nations quietly shared the island without resolving the underlying title. The British Crown chartered the powerful Hudson's Bay Company to establish the Belle Vue Sheep Farm, grazing thousands of prize sheep across the open meadows, while American homesteaders cleared small plots, built split-rail timber cabins, and planted potatoes, with neither side agreeing on who possessed the legal right to govern the territory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CRIME IN THE POTATO PATCH
On the bright, sunny morning of June fifteenth, eighteen fifty-nine, an American homesteader named Lyman Cutlar walked out of his split-rail cabin to inspect his garden. Cutlar was an earnest, hardworking settler from Kentucky who had spent weeks breaking the rocky sod to plant a precious half-acre patch of Norfolk potatoes in the rich glacial soil. To his absolute fury, he discovered a large, black Berkshire boar belonging to Charles Griffin, the manager of the Hudson's Bay Company sheep station, rooting furiously through the rows, destroying the young potato vines, and happily gorging itself on his crop. Cutlar had repeatedly warned Griffin to keep his livestock contained, but the British manager had dismissed the complaints with aristocratic indifference. In a flash of frontier temper, Cutlar grabbed his loaded hunting rifle, took aim behind the boar's ear, and fired, dropping the prize pig dead in the furrows. Realizing almost immediately that he had acted rashly, Cutlar walked two miles across the grassy hills to the Hudson's Bay Company trading post to make amends. He found Charles Griffin and offered him ten dollars in gold compensation—a generous market price for an ordinary hog on the frontier. Griffin was incandescent with rage, roaring that this was no ordinary hog, but a prized breeding boar imported directly from England, worth at least one hundred dollars. Cutlar balked at the preposterous sum, shouting defensively: 'It was eating my potatoes!' Griffin sneered with colonial disdain, snapping back: 'It is not your potatoes, sir, and you are a lawless squatter trespassing on Hudson's Bay Company land!' British colonial authorities in Victoria on Vancouver Island issued an immediate warrant for Cutlar's arrest. Alexander Dallas, chief factor of the Hudson's Bay Company and son-in-law of Governor James Douglas, personally sailed to San Juan Island, threatening Cutlar that British constables would land with armed marines to haul him off to a British jail to face trial for criminal destruction of property.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: ENTER GEORGE PICKETT
Terrified of being seized by British constables and imprisoned in a colonial dungeon in Victoria, the American settlers held an emergency meeting, drafting an urgent petition for military protection to Brigadier General William S. Harney, commander of the U.S. Army's Department of Oregon. General Harney was a legendary, hot-tempered frontier warrior who harbored an intense, lifelong hatred of the British Empire dating back to the War of eighteen twelve. Viewing the British arrest threat as an intolerable insult to the American flag, Harney acted with reckless unilateralism. Without consulting the War Department, Secretary of War John Floyd, or President James Buchanan, Harney dispatched Company D of the Ninth U.S. Infantry, commanded by thirty-four-year-old Captain George Edward Pickett—the very same flamboyant Virginia officer who would lead the tragic Confederate charge at Gettysburg four years later. Pickett had distinguished himself in the Mexican-American War, being the first officer to scale the parapets at Chapultepec, and he relished the prospect of military glory. On July twenty-seventh, eighteen fifty-nine, Pickett landed on the southern bluffs of San Juan Island with sixty-six soldiers aboard the transport steamer Massachusetts. Unfurling a massive American Stars and Stripes over the harbor, Pickett issued a defiant military proclamation declaring San Juan Island sovereign United States territory and announcing that only American civil and criminal law applied. Pickett positioned his encampment on the high ground overlooking the British sheep station, ordered his infantrymen to dig deep earthen breastworks, and placed his troops on continuous combat readiness with bayonets fixed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: FIVE WARSHIPS VS. EARTHEN REDOUBT
The reaction across the strait in Victoria was explosive. Sir James Douglas, the autocratic royal Governor of British Columbia, viewed Pickett's landing as an armed invasion of the British Empire. Governor Douglas immediately ordered the Royal Navy's Pacific Station to intervene with overwhelming force. Within days, five colossal British warships—including the thirty-one-gun steam frigate HMS Tribune, the corvette Satellite, and the surveying vessel Plumper—sailed into San Juan Harbor, dropping heavy iron anchors within broadside cannon range of Pickett's camp. The British battle fleet bristled with one hundred and sixty-seven heavy naval guns and was manned by over two thousand Royal Marines and bluejackets under Captain Geoffrey Hornby. Pickett and his tiny garrison were hopelessly outgunned, outnumbered thirty to one, and within range of explosive naval shells that could level their camp in seconds. Yet, the flamboyant young Virginian refused to yield an inch of ground. Pickett hauled three brass field howitzers to the ridge, established a battery, and told his men that if the British landed, they would fight to the last bullet and make a 'Bunker Hill of it.' Pickett received reinforcement from Captain Silas Casey, bringing the American force to four hundred and sixty-one men with fourteen field guns. When British naval officers came ashore under a white flag of truce to warn Pickett that Royal Marines would land by force, Pickett replied with icy resolve: 'We will open fire the moment a British boot touches the sand.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ADMIRAL WHO SAID NO
The entire Western world was brought to the brink of a cataclysmic war by the stubborn standoff on the bluffs of San Juan Island. Governor Douglas sent repeated, frantic dispatches to the supreme commander of the British naval fleet, Rear Admiral Robert Lambert Baynes aboard the flagship HMS Ganges, ordering him to land the Royal Marines, storm Pickett's earthen redoubt, and expel the American infantry by force of arms. Admiral Baynes, however, was a seasoned, temperate officer who had witnessed the grim carnage of the Napoleonic Wars. He read Governor Douglas's bellicose orders and flatly refused to obey them. Baynes famously wrote in his official journal that two great civilized Christian nations would not butcher thousands of young men and plunge the world into a catastrophic global war over an errant pig in a potato patch. Baynes kept his gun ports shuttered, ordered his officers to avoid any provocation, and forbade the landing of troops. When news of the crisis finally reached Washington, D.C. and London months later via steamship and overland telegraph, both governments were utterly appalled. President James Buchanan moved swiftly to de-escalate the tension, dispatching Lieutenant General Winfield Scott—the supreme commanding general of the U.S. Army—to negotiate a peaceful resolution. Scott and British officials quickly agreed on a sensible compromise: Captain Pickett was reassigned, General Harney was reprimanded, and both nations agreed to a joint military occupation, maintaining tiny, one-hundred-man garrisons on opposite ends of the island until diplomatic negotiations could resolve the border.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE KAISER'S VERDICT
For the next twelve years, San Juan Island was the setting for the most peaceful, polite military standoff in the history of warfare. The British Royal Marines established English Camp on the sheltered waters of Garrison Bay in the north, constructing tidy white barracks, formal parade grounds, and exquisite English rose gardens. The American garrison maintained American Camp on the windswept prairie bluffs of the south. The soldiers on both sides became close friends rather than enemies. British marines and American soldiers regularly visited each other's mess halls, competed in baseball, cricket, and foot races, and shared lavish banquets celebrating Queen Victoria's birthday on May twenty-fourth and American Independence Day on the Fourth of July. Finally, under the landmark Treaty of Washington in eighteen seventy-one, the United States and Great Britain agreed to submit the San Juan boundary dispute to binding international arbitration under Kaiser Wilhelm I of Germany. A distinguished commission of three German geographers, jurists, and historians examined the treaty text and hydrographic charts for nearly a year. On October twenty-first, eighteen seventy-two, Kaiser Wilhelm delivered his official ruling: Haro Strait was the intended channel, and San Juan Island belonged rightfully to the United States. The British Royal Marines lowered the Union Jack with full military honors, toasted their American counterparts with fine scotch, and sailed peacefully away. In an international boundary crisis that lasted thirteen years, mobilized warships, and brought global empires to the brink of catastrophe, not a single human life was lost. The only casualty of the Pig War was the pig.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Pig War of 1859 remains one of history's most delightfully absurd international crises. It stands as an enduring testament to what happens when common sense and cool restraint triumph over bluster and jingoism, proving that sometimes, the greatest act of military leadership is having the wisdom not to fire. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.
